client: I've been struggling a lot since my mom passed away six months ago — it was so sudden, and I feel like I'm still stuck in this fog while everyone around me has just... moved on with their lives. My friends invite me out and try to act normal, but when I'm with them I feel this weird distance, like we're speaking different languages now. I guess I came here because I didn't know what else to do, but honestly I'm not sure talking about it is going to change how alone I feel.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds incredibly heavy — losing your mom so suddenly, and then feeling like the world just kept moving while you're still standing in that moment of loss. That sense of speaking a different language than the people around you makes so much sense, because in a way you *are* living in a different reality right now, one they haven't had to enter yet. I'm really glad you took this step even through the doubt, and I'm curious — when you imagine what "not feeling so alone" would actually look like for you, what comes to mind?

client: Honestly, when I try to picture it, the first thing that comes to mind is just... being able to talk about her without feeling like I'm making everyone uncomfortable. Like, my friends get this look on their faces when I bring her up, almost like they're relieved when the subject changes, and that makes me feel like I have to hide the biggest thing that's happening inside me. I guess not feeling alone would mean someone actually wanting to hear about her, not just tolerating it.
therapist: There's something really profound in what you just said — that not feeling alone isn't about having more people around, it's about having a space where *she* is welcome, where you don't have to shrink the most important thing in your life to make others comfortable. That need to hide your grief can quietly become its own kind of loss on top of loss. I'd love to hear more about her — what's something you wish you could talk about freely that you've been holding back?

client: There's this thing she used to do where she'd call me every Sunday morning, just to talk about nothing really — what she'd cooked, something she saw on TV, whatever was on her mind. And I haven't been able to tell anyone that Sundays are now the worst day of the week for me, that I sometimes just sit by my phone feeling stupid for almost expecting it to ring. I don't know, saying it out loud just now feels strange, like I've been carrying that specific thing completely alone until this second.
therapist: What you just shared about Sundays is so tender and so real — sitting by the phone isn't "stupid" at all, it's your love for her still showing up right on schedule, because that ritual was a living part of your connection with her. The fact that you've been carrying that specific ache completely alone until this moment says a lot about how much you've been protecting everyone else at the cost of your own grief. I'm wondering — now that you've said it out loud, what does it feel like to have that particular thing finally witnessed?

client: It feels... relieving, I think, but also kind of unsettling, like I've opened a door I've been keeping shut and now I don't know what's behind it. Part of me is glad someone finally heard it without flinching, but another part of me is wondering if this is just going to make Sundays harder, you know, now that I've actually named it. I guess I'm a little scared that talking about it more is going to make the pain bigger instead of smaller.
therapist: That fear makes a lot of sense — there's a common belief that if we open the door to pain, it will flood and overwhelm us, but what CBT research actually shows is that naming something tends to make it more manageable over time, not larger, because you're no longer spending energy keeping that door shut. What you just experienced — that mix of relief and unease — is actually a really healthy sign that something real is moving, not breaking. I'm curious, when you sit with both of those feelings right now, which one feels just a little bit stronger?

client: If I'm being honest, the relief feels a little stronger right now, but I'm also skeptical about the research thing you mentioned — like, that sounds good in theory, but I've heard people say "just talk about it" before and it didn't really help. I think what feels different here is that you actually asked about her specifically, about the Sunday calls, rather than just asking how I'm "coping" or "processing," which always feels so clinical and empty to me. So maybe it's less about the talking itself and more about whether someone actually wants to know who she was.
therapist: Your skepticism is completely fair — "just talk about it" without real curiosity about *her* as a person probably did feel hollow, and you've identified something really important: that what heals isn't venting into a void, it's being truly known, and that includes her being known too. That insight actually tells me a lot about what you need in this process — not to "process grief" in the abstract, but to have her life and who she was treated as worth knowing. So I'd love to keep that door open — what's something about her that you think most people in your life never really got to understand?

client: She was really funny, actually, in this dry, understated way that you'd miss if you weren't paying attention, and I don't think anyone outside our family ever really saw that side of her. Most people just knew her as this quiet, reliable woman, but she'd say these things that would make me laugh for days, and now I feel like that version of her is just... disappearing because I'm one of the only people who held it. That's maybe the loneliest part — feeling like her full self only lives in me now, and I don't have anyone to share that with.
therapist: That image of you being one of the last keepers of her dry, secret humor is genuinely beautiful and genuinely heartbreaking at the same time — you're not just grieving her, you're also carrying the weight of preserving who she *really* was. That version of her isn't disappearing though, because you just shared her with me, and now I know she was funny in a way you had to be paying attention to catch. Can you tell me one of those things she said that made you laugh for days?

client: There was this one time I was complaining to her about a coworker who kept taking credit for my ideas at work, going on and on about it, and after listening patiently for like ten minutes she just said, "Well, at least someone thinks your ideas are worth stealing." I was so caught off guard that I laughed until I cried, and then she just went back to talking about her soup like nothing happened. I haven't let myself think about that memory in months because it felt too sharp, but telling it to you just now, I actually almost smiled.
therapist: She sounds absolutely wonderful — that perfect timing, the deadpan delivery, then straight back to the soup like she hadn't just said something brilliant, that's a specific kind of genius. And I want to gently point something out: you just let yourself think about a memory you've been avoiding for months, and instead of it breaking you, it almost made you smile — that's not nothing, that's actually significant. I'm wondering if part of what might help you through this is finding small ways to keep *her* humor alive, not as a way of holding on painfully, but as a way of honoring that secret funny version of her that you were lucky enough to really know — what do you think she would say about how carefully you've been protecting her memory?

client: Honestly, she'd probably say something like "you're being very dramatic about this" and then change the subject, which makes me want to laugh and cry at the same time just imagining it. But when you ask about keeping her humor alive, I'm not sure what that actually looks like in practice — like, I can't exactly tell that coworker story to my friends because they'd probably just say "aw, she sounds sweet" and move on, which would feel worse than not sharing it at all. I think that's the thing I keep running into, that the people in my life don't have the context to really receive her the way she deserves.
therapist: She would absolutely say that, and the fact that you can hear her voice so clearly saying it means she's more alive in you than you might realize. What you're describing about your friends — that fear of sharing her and getting a response that flattens her — is a real and valid concern, not just avoidance, and it makes sense that you'd protect her story from spaces that can't hold it properly. I'm wondering if part of what we could explore together is finding or creating at least one space — maybe even this one — where she *can* be received the way she deserves, so that keeping her alive doesn't have to feel so solitary?

client: This space already feels different from what I expected when I walked in, and I think I'm open to that, but I'm also a little worried about becoming dependent on this being the only place I can talk about her. Like, what happens between sessions when it's Sunday morning and the phone doesn't ring — I can't exactly call you, and I'll still be sitting there with all of it alone. I guess I'm wondering if anything we do here can actually reach into those moments, or if this just becomes another place that helps for an hour and then the walls close back in.
therapist: That's such an honest and important concern, and it actually shows real wisdom — the goal here was never to become the only place she gets to live, but to use this space to build something you can carry *with* you into those Sunday mornings. A lot of what we can work on together is creating small, concrete anchors for those moments — things that are genuinely yours, not just coping strategies that feel hollow, but ways of being with her that feel true to who she actually was. I'm wondering, when you imagine this Sunday morning and you're sitting with that silence, what do you think she would have wanted you to do with it?

client: That's actually a question I haven't let myself ask before, and sitting with it now... I think she probably would have wanted me to make something good to eat and call someone I love, because that's what she did every Sunday — she wasn't someone who sat in sadness if she could help it. But here's where I get stuck: the person I most want to call on Sundays was her, and calling someone else feels like I'm just trying to fill a hole that has her exact shape, which feels almost disrespectful somehow. I don't know if that makes sense or if I'm just making it harder than it needs to be.
therapist: It makes complete sense, and you're not making it harder than it needs to be — you're being faithful to the realness of what you lost, and that instinct to protect the shape of her absence is actually a form of love. But I want to gently offer another way to look at it: calling someone you love on a Sunday morning wouldn't be filling a hole with a substitute, it might actually be *doing what she taught you* — she showed you that Sundays are for connection, and passing that on is less like replacing her and more like carrying her forward. What do you think she'd make of the idea that honoring her might look like living out something she modeled for you?
